## This Course Has a New Home

PSYC 405 was developed by **Patrick E. McKnight, Ph.D.** as an experiment in what happens when you lure students into learning without them realizing they're doing it. Watch a film, have a conversation, read the science, take a quiz — and somewhere in there, you've learned to see human behavior differently. The experiment worked. The [student evaluations](PAST_REVIEWS.qmd) tell the story.

Dr. McKnight is no longer teaching PSYC 405, but the course will continue under other capable faculty in the Psychology Department. If you're looking for it, you'll find it — just in a different format with a different instructor.

Meanwhile, Dr. McKnight has moved on to his next experiment.

**[Check out Peak Performance →](https://gmu-peak-performance.netlify.app/){target="_blank"}**
:::

## What This Course Was About

PSYC 405 was my brainchild — an attempt to test whether you could teach rigorous psychological science through film and have students not only learn it but *want* to learn it. The approach is something I think of as **slipped learning**: set up conditions where real engagement with difficult material feels like the natural thing to do, not the required thing to do.

Students watched films — carefully selected, psychologically rich films — and then did the hard work of figuring out what they'd actually seen. Not plot summaries. Not movie reviews. Psychological analysis grounded in primary research. The trick was that by the time students realized they were reading Kahneman and Bandura and debating the reliability of eyewitness memory, they were already hooked.

### Modules

**Module 1: Mystery** — Perception, memory, and deception through psychological thrillers and detective stories.

**Module 2: Madness** — Psychological disorders, their media representation, and scientific understanding.

**Module 3: Murder** — Criminal psychology, moral reasoning, and justice through behavioral science.

### Governing Areas of Inquiry

Throughout the course, films were examined through six psychological lenses:

1. **BELIEF** — Why do people believe weird things?
2. **PURPOSE** — What will people do to protect their beliefs?
3. **MOTIVATION** — What drives people to act?
4. **UNCERTAINTY** — How do people handle the unknown?
5. **DISCOMFORT** — What will people do for comfort?
6. **EMOTION** — How much do emotions drive behavior?

## What's Next

::: {.callout-tip}
## Peak Performance — Spring 2027

I'm always experimenting. PSYC 405 was my experiment in slipped learning through film. The next experiment is **Peak Performance** — a course about the science of what separates exceptional performers from competent ones across sport, the arts, medicine, business, and tactical professions.

Same philosophy: primary research over folklore, discussion over lecture, AI encouraged not feared, show up and do the work. The goal is connecting students with the skills and mindset for twenty-first century success — and doing it in a way that brings some positivity to the process.

If anyone would care to question whether I know anything about performance, they're welcome to look me up.

**[Visit the Peak Performance course site →](https://gmu-peak-performance.netlify.app/){target="_blank"}**
:::

## Thank You

To every student who showed up, watched the films, read the articles, spoke up in discussion, and told us what worked and what didn't — thank you. You made this course what it was. The evaluation data on this site exists because you took the time to write thoughtful, honest feedback. That feedback is the best evidence that slipped learning works.

PSYC 405 will be in good hands with the faculty who carry it forward. And if you want to keep working with me, come find me in Peak Performance.

— Patrick
